claims.text: Formation and crystal-structure selection in noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles are controlled by competition between nucleation and growth kinetics.
This kinetic competition is sensitive to differences in elemental diffusivities and decomposition temperatures.
An intermediate-temperature dwell allows slower-diffusing, high-decomposition-temperature components to homogenize with the other constituents during nucleation.
A balanced kinetic regime favors formation of a uniform single-phase solid solution.
Rapid heating causes kinetic mismatches that can lead to phase separation, elemental segregation, or uncontrolled particle morphology.
The initial material consists of noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles containing more than five elements.
Rapid heating and cooling typically produce phase-separated or morphologically uncontrolled particles in this material regime.
The proposed intervention is an intermediate thermal dwell below full decomposition but at a temperature sufficient to activate atomic diffusion, followed by rapid final heating and quenching.
The intermediate dwell will allow all constituents to begin nucleating simultaneously.
The relevant structural mediator is nucleation kinetics governed by the balance among constituent diffusivities and decomposition thresholds.
The dwell reduces compositional gradients by allowing slower-diffusing components to catch up during nucleation.
Reduced compositional gradients cause the metal species to incorporate more uniformly into growing nuclei.
Relative to rapid heating alone, an intermediate dwell will produce a more uniform, better-defined single-phase solid solution with better-controlled crystal structure and morphology.
The hypothesis applies when an alloy contains more than five elements and has significant differences in constituent diffusivities and thermal decomposition temperatures.
The hypothesis is limited to regimes in which kinetic control during nucleation dominates phase formation.
The optimal dwell temperature and duration depend on alloy composition, atomic-scale diffusion, and local thermal conditions.
